passage:
Tuesday: Joseph saved the swing next to his for Reena, like always. She came late, breathless, talking about her new dance class and a girl called Mitali. She stayed five minutes, then ran to the steps where Mitali was waiting.
Friday: Reena didn't come to the swings at all. Joseph kicked the gravel and went over everything. Was it because he'd laughed when she fell in the relay race? Because his tiffin smelled of fish? He couldn't find the thing he did.
The next Wednesday: At home, he told his mother, "Reena doesn't like me any more."
Amma asked, "Did she say that?"
He thought about it. She hadn't. She'd just been busy, rushing off to dance practice twice a week with Mitali. Somehow that felt a little better, and still a bit sad.

qa.q: What did Joseph save for Reena on Tuesday?
qa.a: Joseph saved the swing next to his for Reena.

qa.q: What was Joseph worried about as he went over everything on Friday?
qa.a: Joseph worried he had done something wrong to make Reena leave, like laughing when she fell in the relay or his tiffin smelling of fish. 😔

qa.q: What helped Joseph at this stage, and what else could he try?
qa.a: Amma's question helped Joseph see that Reena never said she disliked him; next he could ask Reena to the swings on a day without dance practice.

qa.q: What might Reena be experiencing during these weeks?
qa.a: Reena is probably excited and busy with her dance class and Mitali, and may not notice that Joseph is still waiting at the swings.

grounding: Shows a boy left behind by a drifting friend, wondering what he did, when the real cause is her new dance class and new company.

passage:
Your Dadu will tell you something, beta. When I was eleven, in Nashik, my best friend was Madhav. Every evening in January we flew kites from his terrace, shouting till our mothers called us down.
Then Madhav joined an evening tuition, and after that the colony cricket team. First he came up to the terrace every day, then twice a week, then not at all. Nobody fought. Nobody said anything.
I was sure I must have done something. I remembered the time I tore his best kite and wondered if he'd been angry all along. Every evening at five I felt a heavy, dull feeling in my stomach.
Years later, at a wedding, I asked him. He blinked. "Darshan? You? I was just so tired from tuition, yaar. I thought you'd found new friends."
So when your friend stops calling, don't decide too quickly that it's you.

qa.q: Where did Darshan and Madhav fly kites every evening in January?
qa.a: They flew kites from Madhav's terrace every evening in January.

qa.q: Why did Darshan feel heavy every evening at five?
qa.a: Darshan missed Madhav and was sure he had done something wrong, even wondering if the torn kite had made Madhav angry all along.

qa.q: What turning point does Darshan want the grandchild to take from this?
qa.a: Not to decide too quickly that a fading friend is rejecting you; asking gently, or waiting before blaming yourself, can show the real reason.

qa.q: How did Madhav see the same months?
qa.a: Madhav was just tired from tuition and busy with cricket, and even thought Darshan had found new friends, so there was no rejection on his side.

grounding: Illustrates a boy left behind by a fading friendship who assumes he did something wrong, when the real cause was his friend's busier days.
